summary:
S. 4828, the "Declaration of Independence Reaffirmation Act of 2026," is a Senate-passed bill (considered and passed June 18, 2026) whose sole operative purpose is to reaffirm and re-adopt the Declaration of Independence as an Organic Law of the United States. The bill is declaratory and commemorative in character; it creates no new statutory authority, appropriates no funds, and amends no provision of the U.S. Code or any named prior Act.

Section 1 provides the short title.

Section 2 sets forth ten congressional findings, including that the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration on July 4, 1776; that the Declaration is recognized among the Organic Laws of the United States; that the Northwest Ordinance was adopted by the Congress of the Confederation in 1787 and reenacted by the First Congress in 1789 to retain effect under the Constitution; that Congress has authority to recognize, reaffirm, and carry forward the foundational laws and principles of the American political order; and that the 250th anniversary of American independence occasions reaffirmation of the Declaration as the charter of American sovereignty, natural rights, equal citizenship, and government by consent. The findings further characterize the Declaration and Constitution as together establishing a political order in which the people are sovereign, and describe Americans as "one people" with the right to self-government, national independence, and the securing of their citizens' rights.

Section 3 is the operative provision: "Congress reaffirms and re-adopts the Declaration of Independence as an Organic Law of the United States and as the enduring charter of American independence, national sovereignty, natural rights, equal citizenship, and government by consent." The provision effects a reaffirmation and re-adoption but prescribes no implementing mechanism, enforcement authority, rulemaking directive, or private right of action.

Section 4, expressly framed as commemorating the 250th anniversary of American independence, sets forth verbatim the full text of the Declaration of Independence, from the preamble through the enumerated grievances and the concluding declaration of independence.

The bill contains no effective-date provision, no deadlines, no sunset, no conditions precedent, and no authorization or appropriation of funds. Because it operates solely through findings, a reaffirmation clause, and the recitation of the Declaration's text, its legal effect is confined to the statutory reaffirmation set out in Section 3.
